questions.q: What are the three arguments SUBSTRING takes?
options: The string, the starting position, and the number of characters to extract
The string, a search term, and a replacement
Only the string and a length
The string and two search terms
questions.explain: SUBSTRING(string, start, length) — three arguments, in that order.

options: 1-based — the first character is position 1, not 0
It depends on the column's data type
SUBSTRING doesn't use starting positions at all
questions.explain: T-SQL string positions start counting at 1, unlike many programming languages that start at 0.

questions.q: What does CHARINDEX return when the search term is not found?
questions.explain: CHARINDEX returns 0 for 'not found' — a genuinely different signal from NULL's 'unknown.'

questions.q: In 'SUBSTRING(EmailAddress, 1, CHARINDEX('@', EmailAddress) - 1)', why subtract 1 from CHARINDEX's result?
options: To get the length of everything before the @ symbol, not including the @ itself
To convert the position from 1-based to 0-based
Because CHARINDEX always returns one more than the actual position
It has no effect and is unnecessary
questions.explain: If @ is at position 6, subtracting 1 gives a length of 5 — exactly the characters before the @ symbol.

questions.q: Why combine CHARINDEX with SUBSTRING instead of using SUBSTRING alone?
options: CHARINDEX finds a dynamic position, letting SUBSTRING extract a piece of varying length depending on each row's actual content
SUBSTRING cannot be used without CHARINDEX under any circumstances
CHARINDEX replaces the need for a starting position argument entirely
They must always be used together — SUBSTRING alone is invalid syntax
questions.explain: SUBSTRING alone requires fixed positions; CHARINDEX supplies a position that varies per row, like where '@' falls in each email address.
